utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, our intern, Kyle Wood, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to greet everybody who is present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, as well as the personnel of the Chamber. Before we begin today's sitting with the witness that has been planned, I have three issues to raise on behalf of the Chamber. The first one: Within the next few hours, the Chamber is going to render its decision with regard to Witness 108. You know that there is an expert who was planned to testify as Witness 108. I would kindly ask the parties to read this decision carefully because there are a number of issues that will be connected with tendering exhibits into evidence through this expert witness. The second issue we wish to raise is as follows: We are faced with a request for accepting certain facts. The motion was submitted by the Defence. The Defence is asking from the Chamber to accept certain facts as adjudicated facts. Those concern the events in the Lasva Valley. The Prosecution submitted its answer on the 5th of February; that was last week. The Defence replied to that response, and in the Defence's reply, there are some additional changes. Now I'm turning towards the Prosecution. I would like to hear from the Prosecution what is their position regarding the reply by the Defence and regarding the observations put forward by the Defence in the reply that they submitted on the 5th of February, 2004. Once we hear what the Prosecution thinks, we will render our final decision on this. In this way, we shall resolve the issues with regard to all the submissions that have been submitted, unless there are some submissions in the future. I'm sure that this is going to be the case as well. And now the third issue: At the beginning of these proceedings, on the 3rd of December, 2003, the Defence requested the admission of a videotape featuring the Lasva Valley, and it is an aerial video. This exhibit was marked DH1. We saw this video footage; however this video footage also features some other things. There's a helicopter flying above the Lasva Valley and some other events are depicted. At this moment the Defence has to revise some technical means. They have to revisit that videotape and they have to replace the videotape that was tendered by a videotape which will contain exclusively the view of the Lasva Valley and nothing else. Because in view of what we said the last time with regard to the request of the Prosecution has to apply to the request of the Defence. This was the first exhibit that was tendered, and at that time you did not make copies for all the parties. There was just one videotape. And the Prosecution did not have the opportunity to watch this videotape. I am therefore inviting the Defence to revisit this tape, and if what I've just said is indeed the truth, you have to tender a new tape. You have to show it to the Prosecution first. And we would like to have on this Exhibit, DH1, only a view of the Lasva Valley and nothing else. Maybe at this moment you're not aware of the fact that there are some other elements on that video. The helicopter must have flown a bit further and maybe you have not noticed that. I draw your attention to this issue, as well as to the Prosecution. I invite the Defence to revisit this exhibit, DH1, and to give us a new cassette -- a new videotape. Since you don't have it in front of you, obviously you cannot give us any observations regarding this videotape. If there are no other issues to be raised, we are going to proceed with the witness. But since the protective measures have been granted, we are going to go into private session, and I'm turning to the Prosecution to confirm whether this is the case. Mr. Withopf, did you indeed ask for private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, we are about to ask for private session, Mr. President, and Mr. Mundis will make an oral application for closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. It is ten past 3.00. We are going to suspend this hearing for 20 minutes, and we shall resume at half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall now resume. I would kindly ask Mr. Registrar to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now half past 4.00. We can continue with the next witness. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to bring the witness into the courtroom. Can you please signal, Mr. Registrar, at what point we have to have the next technical break, because I have lost the trace of the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear my words translated into your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called by the Prosecution to testify in this case. Can you please give us your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Berislav Marjanovic. I was born on the 27th of February, 1962 in Paklarevo, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your profession? What do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a farmer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your profession? What did you do ten years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993 I was also a farmer. I was engaged in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. A question that I would like to ask you now, because it's very important for the Trial Chamber: Have you already testified before in the Tribunal or is this the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never been convicted. I have never appeared before any tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not asked you whether you have ever been convicted, I just asked you whether you have ever witnessed or testified in front of a tribunal. Have you ever appeared before a judge as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have never been in a courtroom. I have never testified before any judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is very important for us. Since this is your first testimony before any tribunal, you have to take a solemn declaration. You have to read a text which you are not familiar with, so you will read it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is your first testimony before any judge. You are very far from your own country. I would like to give you some explanations about your testimony. You have been called by the Prosecution. And within these proceedings, the Prosecution, seated on your right, are going to ask you some questions. This examination will last for a while. We are to sit until 7.00. When questions are put to you, please try to answer as completely as possible. If you don't know an answer, you simply say "I don't know." If you don't understand a question, you are allowed to say so and then the question will be rephrased. Whatever difficulties you may have, please tell us. The Judges, which are in front of you, will help you with those difficulties. When you hear a question, think and respond as truthfully and as completely as you can. When the Prosecution is done with their questions, then the Defence, seated on your left - there is six of them, actually, but only two will be asking you questions - they're going to ask you questions based on what you said in response to the Prosecution. Again, you have to be precise in your answers and you have to provide complete answers. Sometimes those questions will be complicated and difficult; at that point, if you think that the questions are difficult, you may state so and the question will be rephrased. If the question is put too fast, you indicate that to us and then the parties will give you enough time to think and to reply. The three Judges, seated in front of you, may also ask for some clarifications. They can also ask you questions. Did you understand all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have to tell you that you have taken the solemn declaration and you have promised to be speaking the truth and nothing but the truth. If you lie to us or if you give us a false testimony, that may put you in danger of being punishable by law. Avoid this and tell us nothing but the truth. If at any point when you're asked a question the Judges don't know what the circumstances were and what you are going to answer, but try to avoid giving answers that may one day be used against you. So you may indicate that there are such questions, that if you answer them the answers may be turned against you. So you have to indicate that to us. In a nutshell, we would like to hear that if you -- at any point in time you have any problems with the questions. The Prosecution is going to examine you first; the Defence is going to cross-examine you; and the Judges also have the right to ask you questions. But you also have your rights, and those rights will be respected. We will now begin. We have to make a break within 40 minutes for a break. It will be Mrs. Benjamin who's going to lead the examination-in-chief. We would like to greet you, Mrs. Benjamin, because you have just joined us. I give you the floor for your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Mr. President, Your Honours, and to Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, you were born in the village of Paklarevo. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber in which municipality is this village situated.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is situated in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you give us the ethnic composition of this village.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The village was inhabited exclusively by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you do compulsory national service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, for 12 months, in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you ever enlisted as a member of any other military organisation or of a village guard?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in a patrol, but not any other army but the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you joined the patrol.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but sometime in April, when we started patrolling. Actually, the Serbs were on Mount Vlasic, and we had patrols to defend ourselves from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you give us the year. April of what year, please?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that the Serbs were near to your village. Could you tell us from April 1992 what transpired with the appearance of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened was the shelling of Paklarevo and surrounding villages, Travnik, Turbe, and the environs. I was walking on foot from my house, and a shell fell behind me and wounded me seriously.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How often did the shelling take place then?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was occasional, but that day was the worst, the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, 1992, you said you were injured while you were walking. Could you state for the Trial Chamber what injuries you suffered.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were shrapnel that hit my right shoulder, head, ribs, and right thigh.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you -- do you recover -- or did you recover from these injuries? Do you have scars from these injuries?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do have scars. When I was injured, I was transferred to the hospital in Travnik. Immediately I was transferred there, and I spent some ten days there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, Mr. President and Your Honours, the witness would like to show the Trial Chamber his scars at this moment, that he suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please indicate to the Trial Chamber the scars that you suffered.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean from the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, please, the ones that you just told us about. Could you show us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. Before he shows anything, the Defence certainly has an objection. And I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has an objection. These injuries occurred before the indictment period, and I don't see that there's any need for the witness to have to be embarrassed by having to show the scars of his injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, either these injuries are directly linked to the indictment or the injuries occurred prior to the indictment period, because in the indictment period the infractions start from January 1993 - January, May, June. Or if these injuries occurred in 1992, he tells us he was injured and we take note of it, but there's no point of him actually testifying about that. So what is the relevance of your question in relation to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the scars are still very much visible, and the scars, the injuries that were received before the indictment are considered in the indictment -- are referred to in the indictment at the time. But if the Trial Chamber feels that it is not necessary, the Prosecution will abide by the ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness told us that he was injured in 1992 and we take note of it, and there's no need for us to have an exposure of his body. If he tells us he was injured, there's no need to challenge that. But as the Defence has rightly noted, it doesn't come within the scope of the acts that the accused have been charged with, because the injuries were caused during a previous period. So you wanted us to learn that he was injured previously, and we take note of that. Now please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, upon your release from the hospital, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were taken to.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I was released from hospital, I was taken to the village of Maljine, because my wife is from that village. And I stayed there for a year. And I went for treatment to Travnik and to Guca Gora, actually, for bandaging of my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So in the beginning of the year 1993, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in the village of Maljine, from the 15th of May 1992, when I was wounded. Then I was discharged from hospital and I was taken to the village of Maljine, and I lived there until the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, could you -- could you state for the Trial Chamber the atmosphere in Maljine in the beginning of 1993 up until when you left. Tell us what Maljine was -- what was about.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere was good, up until June. In May, everything was still okay. In June, what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Something happened in June of 1993 in Maljine. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, in the village of Maljine -- or, rather, the village of Maljine was attacked by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Mujahedin at dawn, about 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning. When they captured the village and there was shooting all around -- I forgot to mention that at dawn there was heavy shelling, first of all, and then came the infantry weapons and the shooting was very loud. And this went on until sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During this time, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was sleeping, and the noise woke me up. I had two children; one was four and a half months old and the other was three and a half years old. I took the kids and fled to the basement because of the shelling. As I looked around, I saw that a couple of stables were on fire, and then I'd go back into the basement and wait for my destiny.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where was your house located in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My house was to the right when you enter the village. Actually, it wasn't my house; it was my brother-in-law's house, but I stayed there. And I could see the rest of the village that was burning and I could hear the shooting and the cries of "Allah-U-Ekber" and "Tekbir."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At that time, were you in possession of a pistol?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had my own personal pistol, which I had brought with me and for which I had a licence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you fire back?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't fire. I didn't even try to fire. I had already been wounded, and what would I do with a pistol?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how you felt at that moment.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I felt troubled, scared. I feared for the children, for my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During that time, did you hear any voices saying anything?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: We could hear them shouting afterwards, "Surrender. Come out of your houses and basements. Those that don't come out will get killed." And there were others in this basement, and we came out. We came down to the village and entered a yard, and we waited there. And then we saw columns passing in the direction of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you have stated to the Trial Chamber that "they told us to come out." Could you tell the Trial Chamber who you refer to when you say "they."

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim army, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you come out?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did come out. All of us came out to a yard in front of a house. Those who had weapons surrendered those weapons. I gave in my personal pistol. And then we waited to leave towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court how many people were in this group and the ethnic composition of the members of the group.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The group consisted of Croats. There were about 50 of us in one group, and some groups had already left before that towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Who escorted your group to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Our group was escorted by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, soldiers of the Muslim army. And we went near to the Bikosi village, and there was a Mujahedin there standing by a Golf car, and he waved with his hand that three of four of us should push his car because he couldn't ignite it. So we pushed the car for a while, until it started going on its own. Then again we joined the column and continued towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On your way to Mehurici, did you pass any particular village?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We passed through the village of Poljanice. And just below that village we came across a group of people that had been turned back from Mehurici. And I was carrying my four and a half month old son, and then the Muslim army and the Mujahedin approached us and they selected some people. I think the oldest one was about 45 years old. And they selected us into this group, and then they turned us back and he snatched the child away from my arms. He gave them to my wife, and my bag, and they continued along to Mehurici; whereas, we were told to go back towards Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During this time on your way to Maljine, were you subjected to any insults, threats, beatings of any sort?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: These people who were shepherding us, three of them had green masks over their heads. They didn't beat us. We came across Ana Pranjes, who was going with her aunt, called Curka - this was probably her nickname and -- the Mujahedin went up to her and she had a Red Cross sign and a camouflage uniform on. And he told her to take off the Red Cross band, and this other one interpreted for him. He said she wouldn't. He tore off the armband, as well as the chain and cross, and he put it in his pocket and then he made her join our group and turned us all back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You said you were turned all back. Could you tell us what direction you were turned to now.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They took us towards Maljine. They said, "We'll see where your trenches are." And as we went, we met in Poljanice a group that was going towards Mehurici. These were four or five wounded people - I don't remember exactly - and a woman, who was on a stretcher. She had been wounded at Maljine the day before, in the leg. They ordered me to carry Sreco Bobas on a wooden piece of fence and to carry him back. He couldn't walk. He had entry and exit wounds in both legs. We carried him to above Poljanice, and there were two or three trenches there. And then a group of some 12 men were selected in front of those trenches, and I thought the worst was about to happen, that they would all be killed, but they didn't come to an agreement and then the group was sent back to join the rest of us and then the column continued towards Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: This group of wounded people that you came upon, were they escorted by any particular set of people?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were escorted by soldiers of the Muslim army, the BH army, and the Mujahedin were among them. And they all came back with us, those who were escorting them and those who were escorting us. And they call accompanied us. They walked on our left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you describe the physical appearance of the persons that you referred to as the Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They had different coloured skin. They couldn't speak. They could just say "Ustasha," and "bojovnik." They didn't know any other words in our language. And they differed from the domestic people, of course, from the locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you finally arrive at Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we reached the village of Bikosi, Mijo Tavic, who suffered from epilepsy, when we reached the houses there he got an attack and he started shouting. And when he started shouting, they opened fire. And when I saw them shooting, I turned around to tell them that he had epilepsy, but I saw that they were gone. I put my hands on my head and fell to the ground. And when I fell to the ground, I saw that my left lower leg was stiff, and I lay on the ground and I saw a young man trying to jump over a fence in a black leather jacket. And he was killed with a burst of fire and he stayed there attached to the fence. I continued lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to your leg that was stiff at that moment.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was shot. I was lying on the ground, and I could only feel my left lower leg getting numb. I was thinking what to do. At that moment, somebody shouted, "Help, I'm wounded." I suppose that one of the soldiers was shooting very low and inflicted a wound on some other soldier and they scattered. But again they reappeared and they shot some of the people in the heads, people who were moving and wriggling too much. They would be shot in the head. There was one young man lying next to me. His legs were over my body. He was shot in the head as well. I was afraid that they would shoot me in the head, but they didn't. I somehow escaped that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During this -- this shooting, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was lying on the road. I was thinking what to do. All of a sudden I hear -- I heard a shout, "Help, are there -- is there anybody alive? I am wounded." I waited for another moment to see whether there was still shooting going on. When I jumped to my feet, three or four other people jumped to their feet. The person who was shouting remained lying on the ground, and then the three or four of us escaped from there towards the village of Postinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, I'd like to take you back to the scene when you were on the ground. Were you able to actually see these people who were on the ground being shot in their heads? Did you actually see it?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them. I saw very well. They remained lying on the ground. Blood poured from their bodies. And they couldn't move. Those who left were the five of us, one after another, and the rest remained lying on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Approximately how many people ended up being in that group?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some seven or eight, as far as I could tell. I'm sure that there must have been seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many shots you heard fired.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard bursts of fire. I don't know how many bursts there were, but there were a lot of rifles opening fire. There were bursts of fire from many rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when the firing ceased, could you tell us how many people were in your group now.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In which group do you mean? Which group are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The final group that came across Poljanice that were lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 30 remained lying on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when the firing ceased, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the shooting stopped, how many people there were? Are you referring to the bodies of the people who remained lying on the road or the ones who survived?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The ones who survived.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Only five of us survived. And we fled towards Postinje village, and then we stopped by some willow trees and we started dressing each other's wounds. And then two men came with rifles from Bila village and they started shouting towards us, "Surrender." I turned around together with Pavo Barac. We started running up a meadow. They shot after us. There was the buzz of bullets, but they missed us. We crossed a river and started walking towards Orasac village. As we came out of a little wood, we heard a rifle burst.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before we go on, could you tell the Trial Chamber, if you can, the names of the people who were with you and what wounds you saw that they had.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Pavo Barac was not wounded. There was Darko Puselja; he had a gunshot wound through the left shoulder and the left side of the ribs. Zeljko Puselja was wounded in one of his arms. I had to hold the wire for him to crawl under. There was also a man called Marijan, whose last name I don't know. He was from a different village. He had a scar on his right hip.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you, what did you have?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in the left lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On your approach to Orasac, could you tell the Trial Chamber what you observed, if you did observe anything at all.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were walking towards Orasac, and we came to a thick spruce trees. That was the safest. There was a road that leads from Orasac to Han Bila and the old Bila village. Actually, the road went to Han Bila. I'm not familiar with the terrain. And we saw the village being looted, furniture being driven away in lorries. We stayed for 30 hours there among those trees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to make a 25-minute break. We shall resume at twenty-five to 6.00, and we will continue without a break until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We resume at the envisaged time. It is twenty-five to 6.00. I give the floor to Mrs. Benjamin to continue her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, before the interruption, you indicated to the Court that you had gotten to the point of Orasac. And could you tell the Trial Chamber when you made your escape if there was a particular plan in mind as to exactly where you were you were planning to go to and where were your -- what was your intention and where had you planned to go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop. [Interpretation] We have a problem. The transcript is frozen. There is no interpretation. Let's check what's going on. [In English] Can you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, before the interruption, you related to the Trial Chamber that you had reached the village of Orasac. When you made your escape, did you have a particular plan in mind and what was your intention? Where had you planned to go?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The plan was to go to Guca Gora. We arrived in Guca Gora from Orasac village. It was around half past 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning, on the following morning. There was nobody in Guca Gora. There was just one or two persons. I knocked on a door. The door was locked. There was nobody there. And then we proceeded towards Han Bila. When we arrived close to a forest, there was fire opened on us, and then we turned right towards Kula village -- actually, Sarici village. There was our flag there. We could see the flag. We arrived there. We showed ourselves, and we saw that the HVO was there, and we came to them and they transferred us to the hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you admitted into hospital in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was hospitalised for some ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And were your injuries or your illness diagnosed at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were given injections and tablets and a tetanus prophylactic. That was to prevent our wounds from becoming infected.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But what was the prognosis? What did the doctors find? What did they say was wrong with you?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by what was wrong with me and how I should be treated? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You presented yourself to the hospital, and you told us that you stayed some 10 to 12 days. What did the doctors treat you for when you got to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My left lower leg was treated, because I sustained a gunshot wound through my left lower leg, and this is what I was treated for in the hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you for the benefit of the Court tell us when you received that wound.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And what were you wounded with?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a gunshot injury. I had a bullet through my left lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And by whom were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded by the Muslim army and the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when you were reunited with your family?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My family was detained in Mehurici for 17 days. After the 17 days, there was an exchange in Nova Bila, and that's when I was reunited with them, after 17 days in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you continue to live in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, up to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where you live at present.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Croatia, in a place near Daruvar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you, for the benefit of the Court, tell us how you feel now.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: A bit excited, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the examination-in-chief. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is going to lead their cross-examination tomorrow. But before we adjourn for the day, I would like to ask the witness a very short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the question of the Prosecution, who asked you how you're feeling at the moment, you said that you are a bit excited. Are you excited because you are here or are you excited or upset because of what happened to you? What difference do you make? We don't know whether you are upset or excited because you are here in the courtroom or upset or excited about the events, about what happened to you. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: A lot of things have happened from the moment I was wounded, so I am psychologically upset. And this is the main cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So Prosecution has asked you about your -- the way you were wounded, but when it comes to the medical description of your injury, we have not come very far. You were injured by a bullet. Can you tell us about the trajectory of that bullet. Did it go through the leg? Do you still have the bullet in your leg? Did you have to undergo a surgery to have the bullet removed from your leg?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It went through my leg. I had an entry and an exit wound. I have particle -- asphalt particles in my muscle and also the particles of the bullet shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the doctors who examined you, did they tell you anything about the calibre of the bullet that wounded you?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me anything about the calibre. They only told me that I had a gunshot injury. I don't know what kind of a bullet it was. I believe that it was fired from an automatic rifle, as far as I could tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once you were treated, was -- once your treatment was completed, did you receive the history of your illness, the description of your treatment, or did the doctor tell you orally what had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have the history from 1992 and from 1993, from both times when I was treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the things that happened to you in 1993.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the medical records from 1993, and I have all the findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another short question, because we have some time. I want you to clarify something for us. You said that your family was detained for 17 days. Do I understand you well? Your family was your wife and your children? Was there anybody else in addition to your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My wife, my two children, and my in-laws, and her entire family. They were in her village. The -- all of the villagers were detained, some 280 people altogether from that village were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you confirm that your children, who were minor at the time, were detained for 17 days?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was four-and-a-half months old, and the other one was three-and-a-half years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please clarify for the benefit of the Judge on my right and can you tell us where your wife and your children were detained. Where exactly were they imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When they were exchanged, they told me that they had been in a sports hall in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it was a hall in Mehurici. Your children, who were very young at the time, do they suffer any psychological consequences?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The younger one doesn't want to go back to Bosnia. He doesn't want to visit. He still is afraid. He suffers some fear dating back from that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, you understand that you have to come back for the cross-examination tomorrow. We shall adjourn earlier than usually, because the Defence, who are on your left, are going to ask you questions but they only want to do that tomorrow because they planned for your testimony tomorrow. Your testimony is very important, and the Defence have to ask you good and useful questions in order to arrive at the truth. They therefore need a certain time for preparation. You will be taken back to your hotel. You are not to talk to anybody about your testimony. You're going to come back tomorrow afternoon at quarter past 2.00. And after having been cross-examined by the Defence, you will be able to leave. Your testimony for the time being is over and will resume tomorrow at quarter to 2.00. I would like to ask Madam Usher to take you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I would like to give the registrar my order that has been signed by myself. I would like to give to my legal officer the decision regarding the expert. Unfortunately, this is not going to be registered, because it is already almost 6.00. There's one more decision pending, and that is the decision on the admission of facts. We still have a couple minutes to go back to the issue of the witnesses who may be granted protective measures. The Chamber would like to know when there are witnesses who appear on behalf of the Prosecution or on behalf of the Defence, when their turn comes, the Chamber would like to know as much as possible in advance in writing, and they would like to be aware of all the elements that may be involved in granting protective measures. We would like to be aware of all the elements. The Chamber understands that in some cases it is not possible because problems may arise at the last moment, and we understand that. However, there are certain matters and things that may be anticipated, and we would like to be aware of them in advance and, if possible, in writing because it will enable the Chamber to render a decision in writing. You understand that this may be useful because sometimes this will -- demonstrates elements that we otherwise would not be aware of. Obviously, this will be subject to your possibilities and circumstances, but for the witnesses which are of the paramount importance, we would like to avoid any difficulties in the future. This was just an observation of a technical nature. There are modalities which will allow us to accelerate the proceedings. As far as the planning is concerned, one or two witnesses have been envisaged. And based on the previous experiences, we may say that we may even have three witnesses a day, providing that questions are put about important elements only. However, it depends on the parties to look into that and see whether this is feasible. It is the obligation of the parties to respect certain Rules, but in any case, I believe that we can have as many as three witnesses prepared for one day. Some witnesses will obviously require more time. But it is for both parties to take this into account. So far we've had one or two witnesses a day, and this has been the rhythm so far. It is obvious that it is also very useful to envisage a second witness, because it may speed up things. And I would like to thank the Prosecution for making sure to have a witness on standby. As far as the witnesses are concerned, the witness who will be arriving tomorrow and other witnesses, what have you planned for the rest of the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in that respect, can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session again, so I give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at the beginning of the today's court session you asked about the Prosecution's position on the Defence reply on the matter of adjudicated facts. The Prosecution has noticed with great interest the Defence has withdrawn quite a number of the proposed facts. Otherwise, there is no reason for the Prosecution to change its position. The Prosecution keeps its position as detailed in its filings. I wish, however, to take this opportunity to again emphasise that all facts stemming from the Blaskic trial judgement have been appealed and they continue to be under appeal. The Appeals Chamber has not yet rendered its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification. So the Chamber notes that orally you are telling us that you will not provide any written reply to the response of the Defence and that therefore we can render our own decision now. Is that right? Thank you. You have also conveyed to us that regarding the legal aspect, some of the facts are currently before the Appeals Chamber, to the extent that they have been appealed. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's completely correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the third point that you had to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The third point, Mr. President, Your Honours, is the video footage in relation to the witness Nenad Bogeljic. You certainly do recall that the Prosecution played four distinct portions of a videotape. The Prosecution has made all efforts to get these portions being isolated. These efforts have been successful, and we are now ready to tender the respective CDs into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the CDs at hand? Because if so, we can do it immediately. We can distribute them, which would save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have the CDs ready for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we are going to undertake this technical measure, which consists of providing the CDs to the registrar. And I assume that there should be a copy for everyone. Before giving the floor to the Defence for their remarks about these CDs, I note at this point - but we will certainly have more information after your comments - that we have received CDs which are only visual, without sound, with four clips or sequences, numbered 1, 2, 3, 4; from 1425 to 1735, 19 to 35, 15 25, et cetera. This must be the beginning and the end of the tapes. The times have been indicated on the CDs. What has the Defence to tell us regarding these CDs?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I don't have anything to say now, because the Prosecution informed us earlier on that it was not possible to remove the sound from the CDs. However, on these CDs that we have been given, it is indicated that there is no sound. So our proposal to the Prosecution was that we have a look before these recordings are admitted into evidence, that we review them to make sure that they are the same clips that we saw in the presence of the witness, because of course the Trial Chamber wouldn't like to admit anything else into evidence. For those reasons, we expected the Prosecution to show us these clips in the normal manner, after which we would of course concur with the admission of this exhibit. The next point I wish to make has to do with your suggestion this morning. We will check the tape that we tendered to the Trial Chamber as Exhibit Number 1. And if there are any questions in that connection, we will take the liberty of addressing you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn again to Mr. Withopf. It appears that the Defence understood that there was sound on these tapes. I have just indicated that I read out that there was no sound. Is there sound or not? Because when we saw the clips, there was no sound. So could you inform us additionally about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having anticipated this comment made by Defence, there is no sound on the CDs and we are making efforts to replay the respective portions right now. It will take a few seconds only, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What we could do, to avoid encumbering the Defence -- who have more important things to do like preparing the cross-examination -- so they won't have to review the tape what we could do is to play it straight away on our screens. Then you'll be able to view them yourself, and that will put an end to the debate. That is what the Prosecution is suggesting. Does that meet with the satisfaction of the Defence? In that case, I turn to the technical staff of the Prosecution to ask them to play these tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've seen the first clip. So I assumed it is the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was the second. We can now see the third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the fourth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The four clips have just been played for us. On the part of the Defence, are there any remarks to be made or any points to raise? Very well. Mr. Registrar, will you please give me an exhibit number for these CDs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, P63. This is a Prosecution exhibit. In the future, if there would be similar videos for admission, this is a demonstration of how we should proceed in the interest of gaining time. As we still have some time left, I am looking at the Defence to see whether they have any information to convey to us regarding the activities in connection with the archives. Is everything going well? Are there any difficulties? Can Mr. Bourgon provide us with some information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very quickly, to inform the Chamber that we're in contact with the delegation of the European Union of the Monitoring Mission in Sarajevo. We are going to have access to the documents as of next week, on the 19th and 20th of February, and we can continue our observation on Saturday the 21st; which means that according to the authorities in Sarajevo we will be in possession of the documents for no longer than three days after our consultations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Those are good news, which will allow us to make progress and which will allow the Defence to have in their possession documents which may be of use to them, either during the cross-examination of witnesses that may come in the future or within the framework of exhibits for their own case. Are there any other points that the Defence would like to raise? As we have time, make the best of it. Mr. Dixon, you have nothing to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, no, Your Honour, nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Residovic, you have nothing either?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, having exhausted the agenda for this hearing, I invite everyone to come back tomorrow at 2.15 for the continuation of the witness testimony and his cross-examination. You will have in your possession tomorrow already in the morning the document regarding our ruling on Witness 108. Thank you, and good evening. Until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.17 p.m.,
